nameStory: The "smooth" in this lichen's name refers to its relatively clean, even surface that lacks the powdery coating found on its close relative, the Powdery Axil-bristle Lichen. The "axil-bristle" part comes from tiny, hair-like structures called cilia that emerge from the axils (where lobes meet the main body) - like little bristles poking out from the armpits of the lichen lobes!
description: Smooth Axil-bristle Lichen is a leafy, shield-like lichen that forms spreading patches on tree bark. It grows as overlapping lobes that can span 2-4 inches across, creating rosette-like colonies. The upper surface is typically gray-green to yellowish-green, while the underside is dark brown to black with distinctive root-like structures called rhizines. Unlike some of its relatives, this lichen has a relatively smooth, clean appearance without obvious powdery or granular coatings.

idTips.label: Surface Texture
idTips.description: The upper surface feels smooth and slightly leathery when dry, without the powdery or sorediate coating found on similar species - run your finger gently across it and it should feel relatively clean and even

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Forms spreading patches of overlapping, leaf-like lobes that lie fairly flat against the bark, each lobe typically 0.5-1 inch wide with rounded edges

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Gray-green to yellowish-green when dry, becoming more vibrant green when wet - the color change is quite noticeable after rain

idTips.label: Reproductive Structures
idTips.description: Look for tiny bristle-like hairs (cilia) along the lobe edges, especially where lobes branch - these are best seen with a hand lens and feel slightly rough if you brush them gently

idTips.label: Substrate
idTips.description: Almost exclusively found on tree bark, particularly favoring hardwoods like oak and maple, rarely if ever on rocks or soil

idTips.label: Underside
idTips.description: The bottom surface is dark brown to black with branching, root-like structures (rhizines) that feel slightly fuzzy and help anchor the lichen to bark

habitat: Look for Smooth Axil-bristle Lichen on the bark of hardwood trees throughout New England's forests, particularly on oak, maple, and ash trees. It prefers somewhat sheltered locations in mixed and deciduous forests at low to moderate elevations, often growing alongside other foliose lichens on the same tree trunks. You'll rarely find it in very exposed locations or on conifers.

seasonality.spring: After spring rains, the lichen becomes more vibrant green and pliable, making it easier to examine the smooth texture and flexible lobes. This is an excellent time to observe the color transformation from dry gray-green to wet bright green.
seasonality.summer: During dry summer weather, the lichen appears more gray-green and feels papery or leathery to the touch. The smooth surface texture is most apparent when the lichen is in this drier state.
seasonality.fall: Increased moisture makes the lichen more noticeable against autumn bark colors, and the contrast between its green tones and colorful fall foliage makes it easier to spot on tree trunks.
seasonality.winter: The lichen remains visible and identifiable year-round, often standing out against snow-covered bark. Winter's bare trees make it easier to survey entire trunk surfaces for lichen colonies.

funFact: This lichen can live for over 100 years, growing so slowly that a patch the size of your palm might be older than your grandparents - some large colonies could have been quietly decorating the same tree since before the Civil War!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with its close relative, Powdery Axil-bristle Lichen, but remember the texture trick: if you can brush off a powdery coating with your finger, it's the powdery species, but if the surface stays smooth and clean, you've found the smooth species. Think "smooth stays smooth, powdery puffs off."
compareHints: The key difference from Powdery Axil-bristle Lichen is surface texture - Smooth Axil-bristle lacks the soredia (powdery reproductive structures) that give its relative a dusty, granular feel. While both species have similar growth forms and the characteristic axil-bristles, only the Powdery Axil-bristle will leave a powdery residue on your fingers when touched. Both prefer similar habitats on hardwood bark, so texture is your best field identification tool.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike its close relative the Smooth Axil-bristle Lichen, this species has an obviously powdery, matte surface texture rather than a smooth, somewhat glossy appearance.
